Balita

Peso dips slightly as oil climbs

The peso weakened slightly against the US dollar on Thursday. The PSEi, the main index of the Philippine stock market, slipped 3.28 points to 5,490.13, ending a three-day winning streak. RCBC chief economist Michael Ricafort said global oil prices rose to new one-week highs after Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and reports of vessels hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude, a global oil benchmark, traded at $93.60 a barrel. He also pointed to signals that the BSP may raise interest rates less aggressively, and to new tariffs US President Donald Trump proposed on 14 trading partners. For kababayan in Saudi Arabia: the Houthis warned they would target Jeddah and other Red Sea ports if Saudi Arabia attacks Yemen's port of Hodeidah. The bigger picture is steadier. Ricafort said the peso has still gained against the dollar for nearly a month. Still unknown is whether oil keeps climbing. GMA Money: Peso slips to P63.72:$1 as PSEi snaps 3-day winning streak

Foreign investors were net sellers for a fifth straight session, with net outflows of P252.77 million. PhilStar Business: PSEi snaps 3-day winning streak

Also covering the market close: Inquirer Business: PSEi slips as profit-taking ends 3-day rally

Para sa pamilya: Your dollar padala stretches a little further today, but oil is rising again, so leave room in the budget for fuel and fare changes.

Balita

Bank sees less room to cushion economy

ANZ Research, the research arm of the Australia and New Zealand Banking Group, said in a Thursday report that the Philippines is among the Asian economies most exposed to higher global borrowing costs and higher energy prices, along with India, Indonesia and Thailand. The reason: these countries import much of their energy and have had little share of the global investment boom in artificial intelligence. Inflation, the pace at which prices rise, hit 7.8 percent in October, above the BSP's 2.0 to 4.0 percent target. BSP Governor Eli Remolona Jr. said it could reach 8.0 percent in the coming months. The BSP has raised its key policy rate, the benchmark that guides bank loan rates, by 125 basis points since April (a basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point), bringing it to 5.5 percent. On local investment, ANZ was direct: "The Philippines is an exception, as policy stasis is holding back investment." How far prices go from here depends partly on oil and El Niño. Manila Times Business: PH has less room to support growth

Para sa pamilya: With inflation at 7.8 percent and rates higher, loans cost more and groceries keep rising; build a little extra into the monthly budget.

Balita

3 percent growth still possible, says DEPDev

The economy may still grow 3 percent this year, said Department of Economy, Planning and Development Secretary Arsenio Balisacan, but getting there will be hard. GDP, the total value of what the country produces, grew an average of 2.5 percent from January to September, and only 2.1 percent in the third quarter, the slowest since 2021. The government's goal for the year is 3.5 to 4.5 percent. To reach even the low end, Balisacan said the economy would need to grow "something like six percent" this quarter. He said lower oil prices would be a big boost. Why it matters at home: the oil shock from the Middle East conflict pushed up fuel and other prices and weighed on household spending, the main driver of growth. Not everyone expects a rebound. Pantheon Macroeconomics economist Miguel Chanco sees only 2.3 percent growth this quarter, citing weak household finances. The Development Budget Coordination Committee, which sets the government's growth targets, will review them next month. PhilStar Business: DEPDev: 3% GDP growth still possible this year

Para sa pamilya: Slow growth at home can mean padala carries more of the load; list the fixed monthly bills before holiday spending starts.

Diskarte

Pag-IBIG home sale ends Dec. 31

Pag-IBIG's Acquired Assets Super Sale Part 2, covering foreclosed homes the fund has taken back, offers discounts of up to 30 percent and runs until Dec. 31. Buyers can pay in cash, use short-term installments, or take a Pag-IBIG housing loan of up to 30 years. To take part, create a buyer ID and bid online in the Acquired Assets section of the official Pag-IBIG website. Families already living in one of these properties can ask about the Lease with Option to Purchase Program. This is information on a deadline, not a push to buy. PhilStar Business: Over 18k homebuyers benefit from Pag-IBIG program

GMA Money: Pag-IBIG sells 18,071 foreclosed homes in Jan. to Oct. 2026, up 55%

Para sa pamilya: Super Sale discounts on Pag-IBIG foreclosed homes end Dec. 31; buyer ID and online bidding are on the official Pag-IBIG website.

Iba pang balita

Pag-IBIG goes electronic: Starting Dec. 1, Pag-IBIG will release provident benefit claims and short-term loans (Multi-Purpose and Calamity Loans) electronically, through the Pag-IBIG Loyalty Card Plus or a LANDBANK payroll account. Members are advised to nominate their preferred account and make sure the details are correct. GMA Money: Pag-IBIG shifts to electronic disbursement for loans, claims on Dec. 1, 2026

Faster customs release: The Bureau of Customs removed a mandatory prior clearance for imports such as vehicles, bulk rice and iron and steel, which the Customs chief said could cut cargo processing time by around 3-5 days. GMA Money: BOC drops mandatory pre-clearance for vehicles, rice, steel imports

AirAsia cuts jobs: AirAsia Philippines is reducing its workforce, citing rising jet fuel prices and currency pressures. A PhilStar headline puts the cut at 90 pilots; full details were not available in the coverage we read. Inquirer Business: Rising fuel costs, currency woes force AirAsia layoffs and PhilStar Business: AirAsia Philippines lays off 90 pilots
